beats.say: Welcome to Computer Vision.
In this first module, you'll learn what computer vision is, what makes an image digital, and how a vision system turns pixels into decisions.

scenes.title: Image processing versus computer vision
items: Image in → image out · denoise, sharpen, brighten
Image in → understanding out · “3 people and a car”

beats.say: Computer vision is the part of A I that lets machines understand images and video: recognising objects, finding them, following them, and deciding what to do.
Digital image processing is closely related, but its goal is different.
Image processing takes an image in and gives an image out, like removing noise or adjusting brightness.
Computer vision takes an image in and gives understanding out, like there are three people and a car.
Think of it this way: image processing is cleaning your glasses. Computer vision is recognising your friend across the street.
An image can be described as a function, f of x and y. At each position there's a brightness value, called the intensity, or grey level.
When the positions and values are all finite whole numbers, the image is digital: a grid of pixels, each with a location and a value.
Grayscale uses one number per pixel, usually zero for black up to two hundred and fifty five for white.
Colour, or R G B, uses three numbers: red, green and blue.
Binary uses only zero or one, black or white.
In the course, move over the picture in the lab: bright areas have high numbers, dark areas low ones. That grid of numbers is all the computer really has.
A vision system works in stages.
Acquisition: a camera or sensor captures the scene and turns it into numbers.
Preprocessing: clean the image. Remove noise, fix brightness and contrast, resize.
Feature extraction: find useful patterns, such as edges, corners, textures and shapes.
Recognition: compare those features with learned patterns to identify objects.
Decision making: act on the result. Count, alert, steer, or diagnose.
Images aren't only photos. They can be made with any part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Gamma rays, for nuclear medicine and astronomy.
X rays, for medical scans, airport baggage and circuit board inspection.
Ultraviolet, for microscopy and industrial inspection.
Visible and infrared, for everyday cameras, satellites and night vision.
And microwaves, or radar, for imaging through clouds and at night.
Computer vision is used in healthcare, self driving cars, security, agriculture, manufacturing and forensic video analysis.

scenes.title: Which task is computer vision rather than image processing?
options: Counting people in a CCTV frame
scenes.good: That's right. Counting needs understanding of the content. The others output another image.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Counting needs understanding of the content. The others output another image.

beats.say: Quick check.
Which task is computer vision rather than image processing?
Tap your answer.

scenes.title: You're done when
items: An image is a grid of pixels

beats.say: That's Module 1.
You're done when:
you can tell computer vision from image processing,
explain that a digital image is a grid of pixel values,

and know images come from many kinds of radiation, not just visible light.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 2.
Here you'll see how the eye and the camera form an image, how light and surfaces combine, and how a continuous scene becomes a grid of numbers.

scenes.title: The human eye as a camera

beats.say: Light enters through the cornea and pupil, and the lens focuses it onto the retina. The lens changes shape to stay in focus: thicker for near objects, thinner for far ones.
Cones, about six to seven million, work in bright light and see colour and fine detail. They cluster in the fovea, the centre of sharpest vision.
Rods, about seventy five to a hundred and fifty million, work in dim light and see only shades of grey.
A camera does the same job: a lens focuses light onto a sensor, and each light sensitive cell becomes a pixel.

scenes.title: Illumination times reflectance
scenes.big: f(x, y) = i(x, y) × r(x, y)

beats.say: The light a camera records from a point depends on two things: f equals i times r.
i is illumination, how much light falls on the scene. r is reflectance, how much the surface bounces back, from zero for black velvet to one for snow.
White paper, with reflectance zero point nine, in bright light of a thousand gives nine hundred. In a dim room of fifty, it gives forty five.
The paper didn't change. The illumination did. That's why vision systems must cope with lighting changes.

scenes.title: Sampling and quantization
items: How many pixels · too few → blocky

beats.say: A real scene is continuous. To store it, we make two choices.
Sampling is how many points we measure. It sets the spatial resolution. Too few samples give blocky, jagged images.

Quantization is how many values each point can take. With k bits there are two to the power k grey levels, so eight bits gives two hundred and fifty six. Too few levels cause visible bands, called false contouring.
Storage in bits is width times height times bits per pixel. A one thousand and twenty four square image at eight bits is one megabyte.
When resizing, we estimate new pixels by interpolation: nearest neighbour is fast but blocky, bilinear is smooth, bicubic is smoother but slower.
In the course, try changing the sampling and the number of levels yourself in the lab.

scenes.title: Neighbours and distance
items: N4 (up, down, left, right) · N8 (+ diagonals)

beats.say: Many operations look at a pixel's neighbours.
The four neighbours are up, down, left and right. Add the four diagonals and you get the eight neighbours.
Adjacent pixels form paths, connected pixels form regions, and a region's edge pixels form its boundary.
There are three ways to measure distance. From zero zero to three four, Euclidean distance is five.
City block distance adds the steps across and down: seven.
Chessboard distance takes the larger of the two: four.
Images can also be combined pixel by pixel: adding frames averages away noise, and subtracting two frames reveals what changed.

scenes.title: An 8-bit image is reduced to 3 bits. How many grey levels remain?
scenes.good: That's right. Two to the power three is eight.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Two to the power three is eight.

beats.say: Quick check.
An 8-bit image is reduced to 3 bits. How many grey levels remain?
Tap your answer.

scenes.title: You're done when
items: How the eye forms an image

beats.say: That's Module 2.
You're done when:
you can describe how the eye forms an image, with cones for colour and rods for dim light,
use f equals illumination times reflectance,
explain sampling and quantization and their artefacts,
and describe neighbours, adjacency and distance.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 3.
Now you'll look at how an image is stored: as a matrix of numbers, with properties like resolution, bit depth and channels.
A grayscale image with M rows and N columns is an M by N matrix. The value in each row and column is that pixel's intensity.
By convention, the origin is the top left corner, and y grows downwards.
A colour image is a stack of three such matrices, one per channel. Its shape is height by width by three.
Four properties describe an image.
Resolution is the number of pixels. Nineteen twenty by ten eighty is about two point one million.
Bit depth is bits per channel: one bit for binary, eight bits for the usual two hundred and fifty six levels, sixteen bits for medical and scientific images.
Channels: one for grayscale, three for R G B, four for R G B A, with transparency.
Aspect ratio is width divided by height, like sixteen by nine.
One uncompressed full H D frame is about six point two megabytes. At thirty frames a second, that's about a hundred and eighty six megabytes every second, which is why video is compressed.

scenes.title: Colour to grayscale
scenes.sub: Gray → colour: R = G = B (colour is lost)

beats.say: In R G B, each pixel mixes red, green and blue light. Zero, zero, zero is black. All two hundred and fifty fives is white.
A plain average treats all colours equally, but our eyes are most sensitive to green and least to blue. So the standard formula weights them.
Gray equals zero point two nine nine times red, plus zero point five eight seven times green, plus zero point one one four times blue.
Going back, from gray to colour, just copies the grey value into all three channels. It can't bring back lost colour; that needs a trained model.
In the course, try pure green and pure blue in the lab: same average, very different brightness.

scenes.title: Raster versus vector
items: Grid of pixels · photos · JPEG, PNG · blocky when enlarged
Maths shapes · logos, fonts · SVG · sharp at any size

beats.say: Images come in two kinds.
Raster images are a grid of pixels, like photos, camera frames and scans in J P E G or P N G. They get blocky when enlarged.
Vector images describe shapes with maths, like logos, fonts and diagrams in S V G. They stay sharp at any size.
Computer vision almost always works on raster images. More pixels mean more detail, but more storage and computing: a constant trade off.

scenes.title: The shape of a 640 × 480 RGB image array (height × width × channels) is…
scenes.good: That's right. Rows, which is the height, come first, then columns, then three channels.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Rows, which is the height, come first, then columns, then three channels.

beats.say: Quick check.
The shape of a 640 × 480 RGB image array (height × width × channels) is…
Tap your answer.
That's Module 3.
You're done when:
you can describe an image as a matrix, and colour as three stacked matrices,
explain resolution, bit depth, channels and aspect ratio,
convert colour to grayscale with the weighted formula,
and tell raster from vector graphics.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 4.
Images are matrices, so linear algebra and signal processing carry straight over. Let's build the toolkit.

scenes.title: Scalars, vectors, matrices, tensors
items: More dimensions · a batch of images

beats.say: Four building blocks.
A scalar is a single number, like a pixel value.
A vector is a list of numbers, like a feature vector describing one image.
A matrix is a grid of numbers, like a grayscale image or a set of weights.
A tensor is the same idea in more dimensions, like a colour image or a batch of images.
The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them. One two three, dot four five six, is four plus ten plus eighteen: thirty two.

scenes.title: Matrices as transformations
items: ad − bc = area scale · 0 → no inverse

beats.say: Multiplying a point by a two by two matrix moves it, and every point moves by the same rule. That's a linear transformation.
Some examples: one matrix stretches x by two, another rotates ninety degrees, another shears.
The determinant, a d minus b c, tells how much area is scaled. Negative means mirrored. Zero means everything is squashed onto a line, and there's no inverse.
An eigenvector is a special direction the matrix only stretches, never turns. The eigenvalue is the stretch factor: A times v equals lambda times v.
In the course, try the presets in the lab and watch the dashed eigenvector lines.

scenes.title: P C A: finding the important directions

beats.say: Principal Component Analysis reduces the number of features while keeping as much variance as possible.
First, standardise each feature.
Compute the covariance matrix: how features vary together.
Find its eigenvectors, the principal components, and eigenvalues, the variance along each.
Keep the components with the largest eigenvalues, and project the data onto them.
It's used to compress images, speed up models and visualise data. The downside: the new features are mixtures, and harder to interpret.

scenes.title: Convolution and the Fourier transform
items: Slide a kernel · multiply and add
Low freq = smooth · high freq = detail

beats.say: An image is a two dimensional signal.
Convolution slides a small grid of weights, a kernel, over the image, multiplying and adding at each position. Different kernels blur, sharpen, or find edges.
Low pass filters keep smooth changes; high pass filters keep rapid changes, like edges.
The Fourier transform rewrites an image as a sum of waves. Low frequencies are smooth areas; high frequencies are edges and fine detail.
The Fast Fourier Transform computes it in N log N steps instead of N squared. And convolution in space equals multiplication in frequency, which makes big filters fast.

scenes.title: A matrix has determinant 0. What happens to shapes?
options: They collapse onto a line or point
scenes.good: That's right. Zero area scale means the transform squashes the plane.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Zero area scale means the transform squashes the plane.

beats.say: Quick check.
A matrix has determinant 0. What happens to shapes?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 4.
You're done when:
you can use vectors, matrices and the dot product,
read a two by two matrix as a transformation, with its determinant and eigenvectors,
explain how P C A keeps the directions of greatest variance,
and describe convolution, filtering and the Fourier transform.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 5.
Here you'll meet the Python libraries for computer vision, and learn which one to reach for.

scenes.title: The four main libraries
items: Fast arrays · every image is one

beats.say: Four libraries do most of the work.
Open C V, for image and video processing: read and write images, resize, filter, detect edges, draw boxes, read a webcam.
NumPy, for fast arrays and maths. Every image is a NumPy array underneath.
scikit learn, for classical machine learning: splitting data, models and metrics.
And PyTorch or TensorFlow, for deep learning: building and training C N Ns on G P Us.

scenes.title: Open C V basics
scenes.code:
import cv2
img = cv2.imread("street.jpg")   # NumPy array, (H, W, 3), uint8
print(img.shape)
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
small = cv2.resize(img, (224, 224))
cv2.imwrite("gray.jpg", gray)

beats.say: Here's Open C V in a few lines.
imread loads the image as a NumPy array, with shape height, width, three.
Then convert it to gray, resize it, and write it back to a file.
Watch out: Open C V stores colour as B G R, not R G B. Show it with Matplotlib without converting, and blue skies look orange.
In the course, try it yourself in the lab.
Both work with tensors, arrays that can live on a G P U, and both compute gradients for you during training.
In PyTorch, you build a model, choose a loss and an optimiser, then loop.
Forward pass.
Compute the loss.
Loss dot backward.
Optimizer dot step.
TensorFlow with Keras stacks layers, then calls compile and fit. It has strong deployment tools for phones, browsers and servers.

scenes.title: scikit learn: label or one hot?

beats.say: With scikit learn, you split data with train test split, fit a model, predict, and evaluate with accuracy, F1 score or a confusion matrix.
Categories must become numbers.
Label encoding gives one column, like red zero, green one, blue two. It implies an order, so it suits ordered categories and targets.
One hot encoding gives one column per category, with a single one. No false order, so it suits unordered categories as model inputs.

scenes.title: Colours look wrong when you plot an OpenCV image with Matplotlib. Why?
scenes.good: That's right. Open C V uses B G R order. Convert with c v t Color, B G R to R G B.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Open C V uses B G R order. Convert with c v t Color, B G R to R G B.

beats.say: Quick check.
Colours look wrong when you plot an OpenCV image with Matplotlib. Why?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 5.
You're done when:
you can choose the right library for a task,
load, inspect and convert an image with Open C V, remembering B G R,
know the training loop: forward, loss, backward, step,
and pick label encoding for order, one hot for unordered categories.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 6.
Now you'll enhance images: change each pixel's brightness with simple rules, read histograms, and pick the right colour space.
An intensity transformation changes each pixel using only its own value: s equals T of r.
The negative is two hundred and fifty five minus r. It helps you see white details in dark regions, like X rays.
The log transform brightens dark values strongly and compresses bright ones. It's used to display Fourier spectra.
Gamma raises r to the power gamma. Gamma below one brightens; above one darkens.
Thresholding gives two hundred and fifty five if r is at least T, otherwise zero: a binary image.
A histogram counts how many pixels have each grey level. Its shape tells you about the image.
Bunched on the left means dark. Bunched on the right means bright.
Narrow means low contrast, washed out. Spread across the range means high contrast.
In the course, try the histogram lab yourself.
Histogram equalization spreads the levels out automatically, using the running total, the cumulative histogram.
Each new level is L minus one, times the count of pixels up to that level, divided by the total.
For an eight level image of sixty four pixels, with eight, sixteen and eight pixels in the first three levels, the new levels are about one, three and four. The crowded dark levels get pushed apart.
Local versions, like C L A H E, work on small tiles, bringing out detail in both shadows and highlights.

scenes.title: Enhancement and colour spaces
items: Hue, saturation, value · track a colour

beats.say: Enhancement is subjective: the goal is an image that looks better or is easier to use. Restoration is objective: it models the damage and tries to undo it.
Then choose a colour space that separates what you care about.
R G B, or B G R, for display and storage.
H S V separates hue, saturation and value, so you can pick out a colour regardless of lighting, like tracking a red ball.
LAB matches colour differences to human perception.
And Y C r C b, for video compression and skin detection.

scenes.title: A histogram squeezed into a narrow band means…
scenes.good: That's right. Few levels are used, so the image looks flat.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Few levels are used, so the image looks flat.

beats.say: Quick check.
A histogram squeezed into a narrow band means…
Tap your answer.
That's Module 6.
You're done when:
you can apply negative, log, gamma and threshold transforms,
read brightness and contrast from a histogram,
explain how equalization uses the cumulative histogram,
and choose a colour space for a task.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 7.
Noise is unwanted random variation in pixel values. Here you'll learn to recognise it, and to remove it with spatial filters.
Noise comes from sensors, low light, heat, transmission errors or compression.
Gaussian noise is fine grain everywhere, from sensor electronics and heat.
Salt and pepper noise is random pure white and black dots, from faulty pixels or transmission errors.
Speckle is a grainy pattern that scales with brightness, seen in ultrasound and radar.
Poisson, or shot noise, is grain that's worse in dark images, from counting few photons in low light.
A spatial filter uses a small window, called a kernel or mask, like three by three.
Centre the kernel on a pixel.
Combine the pixels under it, with a weighted sum or the middle value.
Write the result to the output pixel.
Slide to the next pixel and repeat. Borders are handled by padding.
Linear filters use a weighted sum, like the mean filter: one ninth times a three by three grid of ones. Non linear filters use another rule, such as the median.
Which filter should you use?
The mean filter averages neighbours. It reduces Gaussian noise, but blurs edges.
The Gaussian filter is a weighted average where near neighbours count more, for a smoother, more natural blur.
The median filter sorts the neighbourhood and takes the middle value. It removes salt and pepper noise and keeps edges sharper.
The bilateral filter only averages neighbours that are close and similar in brightness, so it smooths flat areas but stops at edges. It's slower.
In the course, try each filter on noisy images in the lab.
Take these neighbourhood values: ten, twelve, eleven, thirteen, two hundred and fifty five, twelve, eleven, ten, twelve.
The mean is about thirty eight: the white dot drags it up. The median is twelve, and the dot vanishes.
There's always a trade off: bigger kernels remove more noise, but blur more detail. P S N R, in decibels, measures how close the result is to the clean image. Higher is better.

scenes.title: Which filter is non-linear?
scenes.good: That's right. Sorting and picking the middle value isn't a weighted sum.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Sorting and picking the middle value isn't a weighted sum.

beats.say: Quick check.
Which filter is non-linear?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 7.
You're done when:
you can recognise Gaussian, salt and pepper, speckle and Poisson noise,
explain how a kernel slides over an image,
choose between mean, Gaussian, median and bilateral filters,
and describe the trade off between smoothing and sharp edges.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 8.
Geometric transformations change where pixels are, not their values.
You'll learn the common transforms, the matrix behind them, and why interpolation is needed.

scenes.title: Six ways to move pixels
items: Turn by θ around a point
Slant, like a pushed deck of cards

beats.say: There are six everyday geometric transformations.
Translation shifts the image by t x and t y.
Rotation turns it by an angle theta around a point.
Scaling resizes it by s x and s y.
Shearing slants it, like pushing the top of a deck of cards sideways.
Reflection mirrors it horizontally or vertically.
And cropping keeps a rectangle. That's just array slicing.
Uses include data augmentation for training, aligning images, correcting camera angle, panoramas, and following objects.

scenes.title: One 2 × 3 matrix for them all
scenes.code:
# [x']   [a  b  tx] [x]
# [y'] = [c  d  ty] [y]
#                   [1]
# Translation: a = d = 1, b = c = 0
# Rotation:    a = cos θ, b = −sin θ, c = sin θ, d = cos θ
# Scaling:     a = sx, d = sy
# Shear in x:  b = shear amount
M = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, angle, scale)
out = cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (w, h))

beats.say: All of those, except cropping, are affine. Straight lines stay straight, and parallel lines stay parallel.
They're written as a two by three matrix. The last column, t x and t y, is the translation.
For rotation, a and d are cos theta, b is minus sin theta, and c is sin theta. For scaling, a is s x and d is s y.
In OpenCV, get rotation matrix two D builds the matrix, and warp affine applies it.
In the course, you can try the affine matrix yourself in the lab.

scenes.title: When parallel lines meet
scenes.quote: Affine: 2 × 3, parallel lines stay parallel. Perspective: 3 × 3 homography, parallel lines may meet.

beats.say: A perspective, or projective, transformation uses a three by three matrix called a homography.
Here parallel lines can meet, like railway tracks in the distance.
Use it to flatten a photo of a document, or to view a road from above.
OpenCV finds it from four matching points, with get perspective transform, then warp perspective.
After a transform, output pixels rarely land exactly on input pixels, so values are estimated by interpolation.
Nearest neighbour copies the closest pixel. Fast, but blocky.
Bilinear blends the four nearest. Smooth, and the usual default.
Bicubic blends the sixteen nearest. Smoothest, but slower.
Watch the limits: content can be pushed off the canvas, empty corners appear, and repeated transforms slowly blur the image.
With OpenCV you'll also often do a few other things.
Resize images.
Normalise pixel values, from zero to two five five down to zero to one, or subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation before feeding a network.
Blur, with a Gaussian blur.
And detect edges, with Canny.
Remember: intensity transformations change values, not positions.

scenes.title: Which transformation can make parallel lines meet?
scenes.good: That's right. Affine transforms preserve parallel lines; perspective does not.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Affine transforms preserve parallel lines; perspective does not.

beats.say: Quick check.
Which transformation can make parallel lines meet?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 8.
You're done when:
geometric transforms move pixels: translate, rotate, scale, shear, reflect and crop,
affine is a two by three matrix, and parallel lines stay parallel,
perspective is a three by three homography, and parallel lines may meet,
and interpolation fills in values: nearest, bilinear or bicubic.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 9.
An edge is where brightness changes quickly: the outline of an object, a shadow line, a texture boundary.
Since edges are about change, edge detectors are built from derivatives.

scenes.title: The gradient
scenes.sub: Magnitude = edge strength · atan2(Gy, Gx) = direction

beats.say: The first derivative, the gradient, is large at an edge.
Its magnitude, the square root of G x squared plus G y squared, says how strong the edge is.
Its direction says which way intensity increases. And the second derivative crosses zero at an edge.
There are several edge operators.
Roberts uses two by two diagonal differences. Very simple, but sensitive to noise.
Prewitt uses three by three differences in x and y, with simple smoothing built in.
Sobel is like Prewitt, with the centre row or column weighted two. It's the common default.
Scharr is Sobel with tuned weights, for more accurate directions.
And the Laplacian, or Laplacian of Gaussian, uses the second derivative to find edges in all directions at once.
In the lab in the course, you can step the kernel across the grid and do one calculation yourself.
Canny is the most widely used detector, and it has four stages.
First, a Gaussian blur to reduce noise.
Second, compute gradient magnitude and direction, with Sobel.
Third, non-maximum suppression, which thins edges to one pixel wide.
Fourth, double threshold and hysteresis: keep strong edges, and weak edges only if they connect to strong ones.
A corner is where intensity changes in two directions. Corners are great landmarks for matching and tracking, because they're easy to find again.
Harris slides a small window and asks how much its contents change when it shifts.
In a flat region, little change in any direction.
On an edge, big change across the edge, little along it.
At a corner, big change in every direction. A large Harris response R means a corner.
Morphological operations change the shape of regions in a binary image, using a small structuring element, like a three by three square.
Erosion shrinks objects and removes small specks.
Dilation grows objects and fills small gaps.
Opening is erosion then dilation: it removes specks and keeps big shapes.
Closing is dilation then erosion: it fills small holes and keeps big shapes.
Otsu's method picks the threshold automatically, choosing the level with the largest between-class variance.
Use the Morphology tab in the lab to draw a shape and try each operation.

scenes.title: You want to remove small white specks but keep the main object's size. Which operation?
scenes.good: That's right. Opening erodes to remove the specks, then dilates to restore the object.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Opening erodes to remove the specks, then dilates to restore the object.

beats.say: Quick check.
You want to remove small white specks but keep the main object's size. Which operation?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 9.
You're done when:
edges are fast intensity changes, and detectors are derivative filters,
Sobel is the default, and Canny is blur, gradient, thin, then hysteresis,
Harris finds corners, where intensity changes in every direction,
and morphology reshapes binary regions, with Otsu picking the threshold.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 10.
To match the same object across two photos, taken from different angles, distances or lighting, we need features that stay recognisable.

scenes.title: Keypoints and descriptors
items: What · a vector describing the patch

beats.say: Two ideas work together.
A keypoint is an interesting, repeatable location, like a corner or blob. It's where.
A descriptor is a vector of numbers describing the patch around it. It's what it looks like.
A good descriptor is invariant: its numbers stay similar when the image is scaled, rotated or brighter.
Matching is then just finding descriptors that are close together.
SIFT works in four stages.
Find scale-space extrema: blur at many scales, subtract neighbours, and find blobs at every size.
Refine keypoint positions, and drop weak or edge-like points.
Give each keypoint its dominant gradient direction, so rotation doesn't matter.
Then build the descriptor: four by four cells, each with an eight bin gradient histogram, making a vector of one hundred and twenty eight numbers.
Here's how the three compare.
SIFT: one hundred and twenty eight floats. Slow, but the most robust. Matched with Euclidean distance.
SURF approximates SIFT with box filters and integral images. Several times faster, slightly less precise.
ORB finds corners with FAST and describes them with BRIEF, a binary string of brightness comparisons. It's matched with Hamming distance, counting differing bits. Fastest, free, and good for phones.
HOG describes a whole window, like a person-sized box, by the directions of its edges. It was the classic feature for pedestrian detection with an S V M.
Resize the window and convert to grayscale, then compute gradients for every pixel.
Divide it into eight by eight pixel cells.
In each cell, build a nine bin histogram of directions, each pixel voting with its magnitude.
Normalise over blocks of two by two cells, so lighting matters less.
Then join everything into one long vector. In the course, you can build a HOG descriptor step by step in the lab.
Let's count. A sixty four by one hundred and twenty eight window has eight by sixteen cells.
Sliding two by two blocks one cell at a time gives seven by fifteen, a hundred and five blocks, each with thirty six numbers.
A hundred and five times thirty six is three thousand, seven hundred and eighty features.
So which descriptor should you pick?
Need the most reliable matches, and speed isn't critical? SIFT.
Real-time on limited hardware? ORB.
Describing the shape of a whole object window for classification? HOG.
Deep networks often learn their own features today, but these remain fast, explainable and useful when data is scarce.

scenes.title: Which descriptor is binary and matched with Hamming distance?
scenes.good: That's right. ORB uses rotated BRIEF, a bit string.
scenes.bad: Not quite. ORB uses rotated BRIEF, a bit string.

beats.say: Quick check.
Which descriptor is binary and matched with Hamming distance?
Tap your answer.
That's Module 10.
You're done when:
a keypoint is where, and a descriptor is what it looks like,
SIFT is robust, SURF is a faster approximation, and ORB is binary and fastest,
HOG goes from gradients to cells, histograms, block normalisation and one vector,
and invariance lets features match across viewpoints and lighting.

Welcome to Module 11.
Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
There are three kinds of machine learning.
Supervised learning uses labelled examples. Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a number.
Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels, like clustering or dimensionality reduction.
Reinforcement learning has an agent learn by trial and error from rewards, like in games or robots.
Every project follows the same workflow: data collection, preprocessing, model development, and evaluation on data the model has never seen.
Here are five classic supervised models.
Linear regression fits a straight line that minimises squared errors.
K nearest neighbours labels a new point by a vote of its k closest training points.
Naive Bayes uses Bayes' rule and assumes features are independent.
A support vector machine finds the boundary with the widest margin between classes.
And a random forest is many decision trees, each trained on a random sample, voting together.

scenes.title: Not too simple, not too complex

beats.say: Underfitting means too simple: poor on training and test data.
Overfitting means memorising the training data, noise and all: great on training, poor on test.
Fixes include more data, simpler models, augmentation, and regularisation. Lasso can set weights to exactly zero; Ridge shrinks all weights smoothly.
Tune hyperparameters with cross-validation: split into k folds, train on k minus one, test on the remaining one, and rotate.

scenes.title: The confusion matrix
scenes.code:
Accuracy    = (TP + TN) ÷ all
Precision   = TP ÷ (TP + FP)
Recall      = TP ÷ (TP + FN)
F1          = 2 × P × R ÷ (P + R)
Specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP)

beats.say: For classification, count four outcomes: true positives, false negatives, false positives, and true negatives.
Precision is true positives over all positive calls: of the alarms, how many were right?
Recall is true positives over all real cases: of the real cases, how many did we find?
F1 is two times precision times recall, over precision plus recall.
In the course, you can explore these metrics in the lab.
A defect detector finds ninety of a hundred real defects, and raises sixty false alarms.
Precision is ninety over a hundred and fifty, which is zero point six. Recall is zero point nine.
So F1 is zero point seven two. Moving the decision threshold trades precision for recall, and on imbalanced data, accuracy misleads.

scenes.title: A model scores 99% on training data and 60% on test data. This is…
scenes.good: That's right. A big gap between training and test performance means the model is memorising.
scenes.bad: Not quite. A big gap between training and test performance means the model is memorising.

beats.say: Quick check.
A model scores 99% on training data and 60% on test data. This is…
Tap your answer.
That's Module 11.
You're done when:
you can follow the workflow from data collection to evaluation,
you know regression, K N N, naive Bayes, S V M and random forests,
you balance bias and variance, regularise and cross-validate,
and you use precision, recall, F1 and A U C, not accuracy alone, on imbalanced data.
Next, try the hands-on lab and take the module quiz in the course.
Welcome to Module 12.
A neuron takes inputs, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function.
Stack neurons into layers, and many hidden layers make deep learning.
Activations add non-linearity, so the network can learn curves, not just straight lines.
ReLU is max of zero and z. It's the default for hidden layers: simple, fast, and it avoids vanishing gradients.
Sigmoid squashes to zero to one, for binary outputs.
Softmax turns scores into probabilities that add to one, for multi-class outputs.
And tanh squashes to minus one to one.
Here's how a network learns.
A forward pass sends data through the layers to a prediction.
The loss measures how wrong it is.
Backpropagation uses the chain rule to find each weight's gradient.
Then gradient descent nudges every weight against its gradient: w becomes w minus the learning rate times the gradient.
Too small a learning rate is painfully slow; too large overshoots and may diverge. Try all of this in the lab in the course.
A convolutional neural network learns small filters, like the Sobel kernel, but with learned numbers.
Convolution layers slide filters to make feature maps. Early layers find edges; deeper ones find textures, parts and objects.
ReLU is applied to every value.
Pooling shrinks each map. Two by two max pooling takes thirty two by thirty two down to sixteen by sixteen.
Flatten, then fully connected layers combine features.
And the output layer uses softmax or sigmoid.

scenes.title: How big is the feature map?

beats.say: Output width is W minus K plus two P, all divided by S, plus one. W is input size, K kernel size, P padding, S stride.
For a thirty two input, five by five kernel, no padding, stride one: thirty two minus five, plus one, is twenty eight.
With padding two, it's thirty two: the same size.
Some famous architectures.
AlexNet, in twenty twelve, won ImageNet and started the deep learning boom.
ResNet's skip connections let networks train with over a hundred layers.
YOLO detects all objects in a single forward pass, with each grid cell responsible for objects centred in it, and non-maximum suppression removing duplicates.
Transfer learning starts from a model pre-trained on a huge dataset. Freeze its layers for feature extraction, or fine-tune some with a small learning rate. It's the usual choice in practice.

scenes.title: What let ResNet train very deep networks?
scenes.good: That's right. Skip connections give gradients a shortcut backwards.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Skip connections give gradients a shortcut backwards.

That's Module 12.
You're done when:
a neuron is a weighted sum plus bias plus activation, and ReLU is the default,
training is forward, loss, backprop, then a gradient descent update,
you can trace a C N N and compute its output sizes,
and you use transfer learning, and know YOLO detects everything in one pass.

Welcome to Module 13.
Object detection looks at one frame and says what's there and where.
Object tracking follows those objects across frames, and keeps a consistent identity for each.
Most modern systems use tracking by detection.
Run a detector, like YOLO, on each frame.
Predict where each existing track should be now.
Associate new detections with existing tracks.
Update matched tracks, start new ones for unmatched detections, and retire tracks lost too long.
Detections are noisy and sometimes missing. The Kalman filter keeps a smooth estimate of position and velocity.
Predict: use the previous position and velocity to guess where the object is now. Uncertainty grows.
Update: when a detection arrives, blend it with the prediction. Uncertainty shrinks.
Prediction alone drifts; measurements alone jitter and vanish. Together they're smooth and robust. You can try the predict and update cycle in the lab in the course.
The new estimate is the prediction plus K times the difference between measurement and prediction. K is the Kalman gain.
Say the prediction is a hundred, with uncertainty four, and the detection is a hundred and ten, with uncertainty one. K is four over five, zero point eight.
So the new estimate is a hundred plus zero point eight times ten: a hundred and eight. Closer to the more trusted detection.
Which detection belongs to which track? Build a cost matrix: rows are tracks, columns are detections.
Costs come from the distance between the Kalman prediction and the detection,
one minus the I o U of their boxes,
and appearance difference.
The Hungarian algorithm finds the one-to-one assignment with the lowest total cost, better than greedily taking the cheapest pair first.
But it always returns the cheapest answer, even if it's wrong. Two similar people close together can swap I Ds. That's an I D switch.

scenes.title: Handling a long occlusion
steps: Restore ID only on strong evidence

beats.say: Occlusion is when a tracked object is hidden, behind a pillar, a car, or another person. It can lose the track, swap I Ds, or give a brand-new I D.
Keep the track in a lost state instead of deleting it.
Let the Kalman filter keep predicting its path.
When a new detection appears, check it's in a plausible place.
Compare its appearance embedding from a re-identification network.
Restore the old I D only if the evidence is strong. In forensic work, a wrong identity is worse than an unresolved one.

scenes.title: Two similar people walk side by side. What risk rises?
scenes.good: That's right. Near-equal costs make the assignment easy to flip.
scenes.bad: Not quite. Near-equal costs make the assignment easy to flip.

Welcome to the case study.
Multimodal large language models can take images as well as text. They turn image patches into tokens, much like a Vision Transformer.
Could they help analyse crime-scene video the way a forensic expert would?
Research by Opeyemi Adeniran, at She Model Tech, asked three questions.
How closely can these models approximate human forensic reasoning?
Which prompting techniques give the most reliable, human-aligned outputs?
And how do differences between models change how well prompting works?
The data was five thousand, seven hundred and fourteen frames from the U C F Crime video dataset, covering eleven crime categories.
Frames were loaded, then encoded.
Ten frames at a time were sent to each model: G P T 4 o, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2 point 0 Flash.
Each returned a structured J S O N answer.
Answers were judged with a ten question forensic rubric, from crime type and timeline to whether the narrative is court-ready.
Eight prompting strategies were compared. Here are some of them.
Zero-shot gives a direct instruction, with no examples.
ReAct cycles through think, act, observe, decide.
Self-consistency runs five independent analyses, then takes a consensus.
Chain of thought uses six reasoning steps, from observation to interpretation.
The others were sequential, least-to-most, iterative, and meta-prompting, where the model writes its own specialised prompts.
Results were scored with accuracy, precision, recall and F1, plus how consistently the models agreed.
G P T 4 o came closest to human forensic reasoning, with F1 zero point six eight six, then Gemini, then Claude.
These F1 scores are macro averages over the eleven categories. That's why G P T 4 o's F1 is lower than the zero point seven one one you'd get from its averaged precision and recall.
ReAct was the most reliable technique across all three models.
G P T 4 o stayed stable whatever the prompt; Claude varied most between techniques. Explore the numbers in the lab in the course.

scenes.title: Measure, don't assume
scenes.quote: How you ask matters as much as which model you use — and results must be measured, not assumed.

beats.say: The study connects much of this course: images as data, deep vision models, evaluation metrics, and careful reasoning about identity and events.
How you ask matters as much as which model you use.

And results must be measured, not assumed, especially when the stakes are legal. Future work includes more crime categories, combining prompting strategies, and making sensitive models more consistent.

scenes.title: Which prompting technique was most reliable across models in the study?
scenes.good: That's right. ReAct had the highest consistency for all three models.
scenes.bad: Not quite. ReAct had the highest consistency for all three models.
